idiom_name: abstract DAO interface + per-store implementations (+ optional DAO factory)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one interface per aggregate in domain terms (create, find by key, find by criteria, update, delete), give it one implementation per store that owns the connection or pool and contains all SQL, dialect and driver code, and carry data across the boundary in plain transfer objects so no handle, cursor or result set escapes. Translate store errors into the application's own error types inside the implementation, and add a factory (or dependency injection) only when the store must be chosen at run time. Keep the interface stable as the store churns: new queries belong to a new method or a query object, never to leaked store details. In async code, expose async methods (async def / suspend fun / Task) and never block the event loop inside the implementation.
pitfalls: Letting result sets, cursors or vendor error codes appear in the interface: clients re-couple to the store and the seam stops being substitutable.
One DAO per table with generic save/delete methods while business code adds ad-hoc query methods per screen - the interface grows with the UI.
Opening a connection per call instead of injecting a pool, which makes the DAO the owner of connection lifetime and leaks descriptors under load.

N+1 query generation: naive implementations that eagerly load related entities one-by-one inside loops, multiplying round-trips; solve with batch fetching, eager loading strategies or DAO-level join methods.
Returning JPA/Hibernate entities or ORM proxy objects from DAO methods, coupling callers to the persistence lifecycle and causing LazyInitializationException outside transactions.
Synchronous blocking I/O inside async/await frameworks, starving the event loop and turning the DAO into a concurrency bottleneck.

Wrong move: assuming swapping the DAO implementation swaps the data store -> the new store's missing transactional guarantees, lazy loading or batch semantics leak into business logic written against the old one -> instead design the interface around the guarantees business code actually depends on and treat a store change as a redesign of that contract, not just a factory swap.

Wrong move: generating one generic CRUD DAO per table because the framework offers it (jOOQ DAO generation, a shared AbstractDao<T>) -> callers route every real query through fetchByX loops or bypass the DAO with raw SQL anyway -> instead keep generated or generic DAOs as a private base class and expose only hand-named, domain-level methods.

Wrong move: pairing DAOs with pure getter/setter entities -> the domain model goes anemic, all behaviour piles into services and the DAO boundary just shuttles row-shaped records -> instead keep invariants and behaviour on the domain objects and let the DAO only own the store crossing.
